\label{thm:transduce laminar tree}
    Let~$\Sigma$ be an extended vocabulary,
    including a unary set predicate name~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace$
    and not including the binary relational symbol~$\mathsf{ancestor}$.
    There exists a non-deterministic \CMSO[2]-transduction~$\tau$
    such that,
    for each laminar set system~$(U,\mathcal{S})$
    represented as the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace\}$-structure~$\mathbb{S}$
    and inducing the laminar tree~$T$ with ${L(T)=U}$,
    and for each $\Sigma$-structure~$\mathbb{A}$
    with~$\mathbb{S}\sqsubseteq\mathbb{A}$,
    $\tau(\mathbb{A})$ is non-empty
    and every output in~$\tau(\mathbb{A})$
    is equal to some $\{\mathsf{ancestor}\}$-structure $\mathbb{T}$ representing~$T$.

\label{lem:node cases in identification}
    Let~$(A,B)$ identify some subset~$S$ of~$V\setminus L$
    through a pair~$(\pi,\sigma)$ of injections having unique request.
    Then,
    for each inner node~$x$,
    exactly one of the three following cases holds:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item
            $x\notin S$,
            $x$ is not requested in~$(\pi,\sigma)$,
            and for each child~$c$ of~$x$,
            $\card{A\cap V(T_c)}=\card{B\cap V(T_c)}$;
        \item
            $x\notin S$,
            $x$ is requested in~$(\pi,\sigma)$,
            and there exists one leaf~$z\in (A\cup B)\cap V(T_x)$
            such that, for each child~$c$ of~$x$,
            $\card{(A\setminus\{z\})\cap V(T_c)}=\card{(B\setminus\{z\})\cap V(T_c)}$;
        \item
            $x\in S$,
            $x$ is requested in~$(\pi,\sigma)$,
            and there exists two leaves
            $a\in A\cap V(T_x)$ and $b\in B\cap V(T_x)$
            such that, for each child~$c$ of~$x$,
            $\card{(A\setminus\{a\})\cap V(T_c)}=\card{(B\setminus\{b\}\cap V(T_c))}$
            and~$\{a,b\}\nsubseteq V(T_c)$.
    \end{enumerate}

By \autoref{lem:transduce laminar tree induced by weakly-partitive family},
    we have a \CMSO[2]-transduction
    which on inputs~$\mathbb{S}$ outputs the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace,\mathsf{ancestor}\}$-structure $\mathbb{S}\sqcup\mathbb{T'}$,
    where~$\mathbb{T'}$ is the~$\{\mathsf{ancestor}\}$-structure modeling~$T$, with $L(T)=U=U_{\mathbb{S}}$.
    It thus remains to define a second \CMSO[2]-transduction
    which outputs~$\mathbb{T}$ from~$\mathbb{S}\sqcup\mathbb{T'}$.
    Actually, an \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-interpretation is enough.
    Indeed, we can define
    an \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-formula~$\phi_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace}$ which selects the inner nodes of~$T$ that are labeled~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace$ by~$\lambda$,
    and an \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-formula~$\phi_{\mathsf{betweeness}}$ which selects triples~$(x,y,z)$ of elements such that~$x<y<z$ or~$z<y<x$.
    In order to define both formulas,
    we use a functional symbol~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(t)$
    which is interpreted as the set~$L(T_t)$,
    and is clearly \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-definable on~$\{\mathsf{ancestor}\}$-structures such as~$\mathbb{T}$.
    Indeed, an element~$z$ belongs to~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(t)$ if and only if\xspace
    it is a leaf and has~$t$ as ancestor.

    According to \autoref{thm:weakly-partitive tree},
    an inner node~$t$ is labeled~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace$
    if and only if\xspace,
    for every two children $s_1,s_2$ of $t$ the set $L(T_{s_1})\cup L(T_{s_2})$ is in $\mathcal{S}$. We can define this in \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace using the following formula:
        $$\phi_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace}(x):=\forall y \forall z\Big(\big(\ensuremath{\mathsf{parent}}\xspace(x,y)\land \ensuremath{\mathsf{parent}}\xspace(x,z)\big)\rightarrow \ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace\big(\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(y)\cup \ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(z)\big)\Big).$$


    Now, according to \autoref{thm:weakly-partitive tree},
    we have~$x<y<z$ or~$z<y<x$ exactly when~$x$, $y$, and~$z$ are three distinct children of some node~$t$
    and the three following properties are satisfied:
    \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
        \item\label{it:not degenerate} $L(T_x)\cup L(T_z)$ is not a member of~$\mathcal{S}$;
        \item\label{it:not prime}\label{it:x+y-z} there exists a member of~$\mathcal{S}$ which includes both~$L(T_x)$ and~$L(T_y)$ but excludes~$L(T_z)$;
        \item\label{it:betweeness}\label{it:y+z-x} there exists a member of~$\mathcal{S}$ which includes both~$L(T_y)$ and~$L(T_z)$ but excludes~$L(T_x)$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Indeed,
    when these conditions are satisfied, $t$ is necessarily labeled $\ensuremath{\mathsf{linear}}\xspace$
    (\autoref{it:not degenerate} asserts that it is not labeled by $\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace$ and, {\em e.g.}, \autoref{it:not prime} that it is not labeled by $\ensuremath{\mathsf{prime}}\xspace$),
    and, among the possible orderings of~$\{x,y,z\}$, only the ones ensuring~$x<y<z$ or~$z<y<x$ are possible
    ($x<z<y$ and~$y<z<x$ are not possible because of \autoref{it:x+y-z},
    and~$y<x<z$ and~$z<x<y$ are not possible because of \autoref{it:y+z-x}).
    Each of these properties is \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-definable:
    \begin{align*}
        \phi_{\mathsf{betweeness}}(x,y,z):=&
            \exists t\Big[ \ensuremath{\mathsf{parent}}\xspace(t,x)\land\ensuremath{\mathsf{parent}}\xspace(t,y)\land\ensuremath{\mathsf{parent}}\xspace(t,z)\land 
            \\*
            &\neg\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace\big(\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(x)\cup\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(z)\big)\land
            \\*
            &\exists S\Big(\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace(S)\land\big(\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(x)\cup\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(y)\big)\subseteq S\land\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(z)\cap S=\emptyset\Big)\land
            \\*
            &\exists S\Big(\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace(S)\land\big(\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(z)\cup\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(y)\big)\subseteq S\land\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(x)\cap S=\emptyset\Big)\Big].
    \end{align*}
    Once~$\phi_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace}$ and~$\phi_{\mathsf{betweeness}}$ are defined,
    our transduction drops the original predicate~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace$
    which is no longer needed in the output~$\mathbb{T}$.

Our first step is to transduce B from G. For this it is sufficient to observe that we can easily define an ensuremathMSOxspace-formula phi_ensuremathBIPARTxspace(X,Y) with two monadic free-variables X and Y which defines bi-joins \X,Y\ of G. Since B is bipartitive we can apply autoreflem:transduce laminar tree induced by weakly-bipartitive family to transduce Gsqcup Bsqcup T from Gsqcup B. First observe that (U,S_a) is a set system as emptysetnotin S_a (since \emptyset,U\notin B), Uin S_a, and \b\in S_a for every bin U (since~\a\inS_a and for~bneq a, \\b\,Usetminus \b\\in B). To argue the second assertion, assume that T is the laminar tree of the set system (U,S_a). First observe that in the set system (U,S_a) the element a is not contained in any set apart from U and \a\ and hence the leaf \a\ is a child of the root U of T. Additionally, the set Usetminus \a\ is in S_a as the bipartition (\a\,Usetminus \a\) is in B by definition and hence Usetminus \a\ is also a child of the root U of T. Let T' be the tree obtained from T by removing node U, making all edges undirected and adding an edge from node \a\ to node Usetminus \a\. Indeed, by our previous observations, T' is an undirected tree. Furthermore, there is a correspondence between elements of U and the leaves of T' (element bin U corresponds to leaf \b\ of T'). To check that T' is indeed the laminar tree of T, we need to verify that for each bipartition \X,Y\ in B there is exactly one edge e of T' such that X=L(T'_1) and Y=L(T'_2) for the two connected components T'_1,T'_2 of T'-e. We say that the edge e implements the bipartition \X,Y\. Assume that \X,Y\ is any bipartition from B. First consider the case that \X,Y\ is the bipartition \\a\,Usetminus\a\\. Then \X,Y\ is clearly implemented by the edge \\a\,Usetminus\a\\ of T'. Now assume that \X,Y\ is any other bipartition in B and assume, without loss of generality, that ain Y. Hence, Xin S_a. Let X' be the parent of X in T. Note that X must be a proper subset of Usetminus \a\ as by our assumption \X,Y\ is not the partition \\a\,Usetminus \a\ and hence X' cannot be U. As we only deleted edge incident to U in our construction of T', \X,X'\ is an edge in T' which clearly implements the bipartition \X,Y\. Finally, every bipartition \X,Y\in B is clearly implemented by only one edge as every inner node of the tree T' has degree at least three. Therefore, T' is the laminar tree of (U,B).

Let $\mathcal{B}$ be a family of bipartitions of a set $U$ and $a\in U$ any element.
    First observe that $(U,\mathcal{S}_a)$ is a set system
    as $\emptyset\notin \mathcal{S}_a$ (since $\{\emptyset,U\}\notin \mathcal{B}$),
    $U\in \mathcal{S}_a$,
    and $\{b\}\in \mathcal{S}_a$ for every $b\in U$ (since~$\{a\}\in\mathcal{S}_a$ and for~$b\neq a$, $\{\{b\},U\setminus \{b\}\}\in \mathcal{B}$).

    To argue the second assertion, assume that $T$ is the laminar tree of the set system $(U,\mathcal{S}_a)$. First observe that in the set system $(U,\mathcal{S}_a)$ the element $a$ is not contained in any set apart from $U$ and $\{a\}$ and hence the leaf $\{a\}$ is a child of the root $U$ of $T$. Additionally, the set $U\setminus \{a\}$ is in $S_a$ as the bipartition $(\{a\},U\setminus \{a\})$ is in $\mathcal{B}$ by definition and hence $U\setminus \{a\}$ is also a child of the root $U$ of $T$. Let $T'$ be the tree obtained from $T$ by removing node $U$, making all edges undirected and adding an edge from node $\{a\}$ to node $U\setminus \{a\}$. Indeed, by our previous observations, $T'$ is an undirected tree. Furthermore, there is a correspondence between elements of $U$ and the leaves of $T'$ (element $b\in U$ corresponds to leaf $\{b\}$ of $T'$). To check that $T'$ is indeed the laminar tree of $T$, we need to verify that for each bipartition $\{X,Y\}$ in $\mathcal{B}$ there is exactly one edge $e$ of $T'$ such that $X=L(T'_1)$ and $Y=L(T'_2)$ for the two connected components $T'_1,T'_2$ of $T'-e$. We say that the edge \emph{$e$ implements the bipartition $\{X,Y\}$}.
    Assume that $\{X,Y\}$ is any bipartition from $\mathcal{B}$. First consider the case that $\{X,Y\}$ is the bipartition $\{\{a\},U\setminus\{a\}\}$. Then $\{X,Y\}$ is clearly implemented by the edge $\{\{a\},U\setminus\{a\}\}$ of $T'$. Now assume that $\{X,Y\}$ is any other bipartition in $\mathcal{B}$ and assume, without loss of generality, that $a\in Y$. Hence, $X\in \mathcal{S}_a$. Let $X'$ be the parent of $X$ in $T$. Note that $X$ must be a proper subset of $U\setminus \{a\}$ as by our assumption $\{X,Y\}$ is not the partition $\{\{a\},U\setminus \{a\}$ and hence $X'$ cannot be $U$. As we only deleted edge incident to $U$ in our construction of $T'$, $\{X,X'\}$ is an edge in $T'$ which clearly implements the bipartition $\{X,Y\}$. Finally, every bipartition $\{X,Y\}\in \mathcal{B}$ is clearly implemented by only one edge as every inner node of the tree $T'$ has degree at least three. Therefore, $T'$ is the laminar tree of $(U,\mathcal{B})$.
